summary: Describes how to add cryptographic signatures and encryption to MIME email data, which is what S/MIME is for. This is version 3. It was replaced by RFC 3851.

plainLanguage.summary: S/MIME adds two things to an email message: a signature that shows who sent it and that it was not changed, and encryption that hides the contents from anyone in the middle. Both use the standard MIME containers, so a signed message is still readable by software that does not understand S/MIME.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email
subtitle: How signatures and encryption are added to MIME messages, and which formats carry them.

tldr.problem: MIME defines how a message body is structured, but it says nothing about who wrote it or whether it was altered. Sending an attachment or a sensitive note over mail gives no assurance to the receiver.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME wraps MIME parts in Cryptographic Message Syntax objects. SignedData carries a digital signature over the canonical form of the content, and EnvelopedData encrypts it under a key shared with each recipient. Both travel inside ordinary MIME types.
tldr.outcome: The document fixes the algorithms every implementation must support, the MIME types and file extensions used, and the order of signing and encrypting. It has been replaced by RFC 3851.

today: RFC 2633 was a Proposed Standard published in June 1999. It has been obsoleted by RFC 3851, which is the current S/MIME Version 3 Message Specification.

sections.title: What S/MIME Adds to MIME
sections.content:
S/MIME, Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Based on the popular Internet MIME standard, it provides the following cryptographic security services for electronic messaging applications: authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin, using digital signatures, and privacy and data security, using encryption.

S/MIME can be used by traditional mail user agents to add cryptographic security services to mail that is sent and to interpret them in mail that is received. However, it is not restricted to mail: it can be used with any transport mechanism that transports MIME data, such as HTTP. As such, S/MIME takes advantage of the object-based features of MIME and allows secure messages to be exchanged in mixed-transport systems. It can also be used in automated message transfer agents that use cryptographic security services that do not require any human intervention, such as the signing of software-generated documents and the encryption of FAX messages sent over the Internet.

The MIME standard provides a general structure for the content type of Internet messages and allows extensions for new content type applications. This memo defines how to create a MIME body part that has been cryptographically enhanced according to CMS, which is derived from PKCS #7, and it defines the application/pkcs7-mime MIME type used to transport those body parts. It also discusses the multipart/signed MIME type for transporting signed messages, and defines the application/pkcs7-signature MIME type.

Most requirements are placed on how receiving agents handle incoming messages, while the recommendations are mostly on how sending agents create outgoing messages. The guiding idea is to be liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send. The separation also comes from the likelihood of S/MIME systems involving software other than traditional mail clients: an automated process that sends an encrypted message might not be able to receive one at all.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME is a layer on top of MIME. It can carry signatures and encryption over any transport that carries MIME, not only mail, and it works in systems where no person is present to approve anything.

sections.title: The Algorithms Every Implementation Must Support
sections.content:
CMS allows a wide variety of options in content and algorithm support, so the RFC sets out a base level of interoperability. Sending and receiving agents MUST support SHA-1 as a digest algorithm, and receiving agents SHOULD support MD5 to give backward compatibility with MD5-digested S/MIME v2 SignedData objects.

For signatures, sending and receiving agents MUST support id-dsa, and the algorithm parameters MUST be absent rather than encoded as NULL. Receiving agents SHOULD support rsaEncryption and sending agents SHOULD support it too, because S/MIME v2 clients are only capable of verifying digital signatures using the rsaEncryption algorithm. For key encryption, sending and receiving agents MUST support Diffie-Hellman, and both SHOULD support rsaEncryption, since S/MIME v2 clients can only decrypt content encryption keys using rsaEncryption.

Only three CMS content types are used for S/MIME: Data, SignedData and EnvelopedData. Sending agents MUST use the signedData content type to apply a digital signature to a message, or, in a degenerate case where there is no signature information, to convey certificates. EnvelopedData is used to apply privacy protection to a message; a sender needs a public key for each intended recipient, and this content type does not provide authentication.

For content encryption, sending and receiving agents MUST support encryption and decryption with DES EDE3 CBC, called tripleDES. Receiving agents SHOULD support RC2 or a compatible algorithm at a key size of 40 bits, called RC2/40. A sending agent decides which algorithm to use from the capabilities list the recipient announced, and falls back through a defined order: known capabilities, then the algorithm used on the last signed and encrypted message received from the recipient, then tripleDES. Before sending, the sending agent MUST decide whether it is willing to use weak encryption for the data in the message; if weak encryption is unacceptable it MUST NOT use an algorithm such as RC2/40.
sections.plainLanguage: To make sure two implementations can talk to each other, the RFC names one algorithm each for hashing, signing, key exchange and encryption that everybody must implement, and lists others that are optional.

sections.title: The MIME Types That Carry the Objects
sections.content:
S/MIME provides one format for enveloped-only data, several formats for signed-only data, and several for signed and enveloped data. The application/pkcs7-mime type carries CMS objects of several types including envelopedData and signedData. Since CMS objects are binary data, in most cases base-64 transfer encoding is appropriate, in particular when used with SMTP transport. The transfer encoding depends on the transport through which the object is sent and is not a characteristic of the MIME type.

The MIME headers of all application/pkcs7-mime objects SHOULD include the optional smime-type parameter, which conveys details about the security applied along with information about the contained content. The memo defines three: enveloped-data for EnvelopedData, signed-data for SignedData, and certs-only for a degenerate SignedData with no content. Sending agents SHOULD also emit the optional name parameter on the Content-Type field and the optional Content-Disposition field with a filename parameter, using the extensions .p7m for signedData and envelopedData, .p7c for a degenerate certs-only message, and .p7s for application/pkcs7-signature. Including a file name makes the objects easier to use as files on disk and can convey type information across gateways, but a proper S/MIME implementation MUST use the MIME types and MUST NOT rely on the file extensions.

The multipart/signed type is a clear-signing format with two parts. The first part contains the MIME entity that is signed, and the second contains the detached signature CMS SignedData object, in which the encapContentInfo eContent field is absent. The second part has the type application/pkcs7-signature and always contains a single CMS object of type signedData. The multipart/signed Content type has two required parameters: protocol, which MUST be application/pkcs7-signature, and micalg, which allows one-pass processing when the signature is verified. Its value depends on the message digest algorithms used, with md5 for MD5, sha1 for SHA-1 and unknown for any other algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The cryptographic objects travel in three familiar MIME containers: a single part that holds the whole object, a two-part message where the text stays readable and the signature sits next to it, and a single part that holds only a signature.

sections.title: Signing, Encrypting and the Order of Operations
sections.content:
The data to be secured is always a canonical MIME entity. The MIME entity and other data, such as certificates and algorithm identifiers, are given to CMS processing facilities which produce a CMS object, and the CMS object is then wrapped in MIME. A single procedure is used for creating MIME entities that are to be signed, enveloped, or both: the MIME entity is prepared according to the local conventions, the leaf parts are converted to canonical form, and appropriate transfer encoding is applied to the leaves.

Each MIME entity MUST be converted to a canonical form that is uniquely and unambiguously representable in the environment where the signature is created and where it will be verified, and MIME entities MUST be canonicalized for enveloping as well as signing. For text, both line endings and character set must be canonicalized, with the line ending being the pair of characters CR LF. If a multipart/signed entity is ever transmitted over standard Internet SMTP infrastructure, it MUST have transfer encoding applied so that it is represented as 7-bit text, because the mail transport cannot guarantee transport of 8-bit or binary data.

To achieve signing and enveloping, any of the signed-only and encrypted-only formats may be nested, because all of the formats are MIME entities and all of them secure MIME entities. An implementation MUST be able to receive and process arbitrarily nested S/MIME within reasonable resource limits. It is possible to sign first or to envelop first. When signing first, the signatories are securely obscured by the enveloping. When enveloping first, the signatories are exposed, but it is possible to verify signatures without removing the enveloping, which is useful where automatic signature verification is desired, since no private key material is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The content is first rewritten into one standard form, so that the signature still checks after the message has travelled. Signing and encryption can be nested in either order, and the order decides whether a reader can check the signature before decrypting.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC notes that 40-bit encryption is considered weak by most cryptographers, and that using weak cryptography in S/MIME offers little actual security over sending plaintext. Using weak cryptography is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography. When feasible, sending and receiving agents should inform senders and recipients of the relative cryptographic strength of messages.

It is impossible for most software or people to estimate the value of a message, or the actual cost of decrypting a message encrypted with a key of a particular size, or the cost of a failed decryption. Choosing between different key sizes, or choosing whether to use plaintext at all, is also impossible. However, such decisions are made all the time, and the memo gives a framework for using those estimates in choosing algorithms.

Two warnings follow. If a sending agent sends the same message using different strengths of cryptography, an attacker watching the communications channel may be able to determine the contents of the strongly encrypted message by decrypting the weakly encrypted version, so a sender should not send a copy of a message using weaker cryptography than they would use for the original. And modification of the ciphertext can go undetected if authentication is not also used, which is the case when sending EnvelopedData without wrapping it in SignedData or enclosing SignedData within it.
sections.plainLanguage: Weak encryption is barely better than no encryption. And sending the same message twice, once weakly encrypted, undoes the strong copy for anyone watching the connection.

viz.caption: THE S/MIME FORMATS AND THEIR FILE EXTENSIONS

items.title: SHA-1 digest
items.text: Required for both sending and receiving agents.

items.title: id-dsa signature
items.text: Required; its algorithm parameters must be absent, not NULL.

items.title: rsaEncryption signature
items.text: Recommended, because S/MIME v2 clients can only verify RSA signatures.

items.title: Diffie-Hellman key encryption
items.text: Required for both sending and receiving agents.

items.title: tripleDES content encryption
items.text: Required: DES in EDE3 CBC mode.

items.title: RC2/40
items.text: Recommended for receivers, but weak; a sender must not use it for sensitive data.

viz.caption: THE TWO ORDERS OF SIGNING AND ENCRYPTING

items.title: Sign, then encrypt
items.text: The signatures are hidden inside the encrypted part. A receiver must decrypt before checking them.

items.title: Encrypt, then sign
items.text: The signature stays visible and can be checked without decrypting and without any private key.

items.title: The catch with encrypt-then-sign
items.text: A careful attacker may change the unauthenticated parts of the encrypted message.

items.title: The catch with sign-then-encrypt
items.text: A receiver can rely on the signed message being unaltered, but cannot relate the signer to the unencrypted contents.
